verdictStatement: Both of Codex's OBJECT blockers and both of my v6 SHOULD-FIX items are answered, and the answers are real work rather than relabelling: the lifecycle is now anchored to the (project, grant generation) carrier permission-truth-tables.v6 actually specifies, operation purge is correctly separated from the two terminalizing events, restore after possible tail loss permanently revokes rather than guessing, and FROZEN-UNDER-OVERTURN gives the already-written bytes a lawful standing instead of stranding them. The succession discipline is clean for the third generation running — 43 changed paths, zero off-roster, 161 of 161 non-roster paths byte-identical — and the v7 re-measurement is correct on all three files at the declared HEAD. The blocker is not a missing repair. It is that the repair introduced a terminalization model whose branches cannot all be obeyed: projectPurge and grantGenerationClosure each MUST emit 'exactly one' terminal marker on the same carrier and each MUST refuse appends afterwards, while three other branches drive that carrier to mandatory append-refusal with no marker at all. Whichever fires first makes the others' MUST unsatisfiable. Codex asked which event terminalizes; the answer given is two events plus three silent terminal states, with no precedence, idempotence, or already-terminal rule between them.

blockers.title: The new terminalization model is jointly unsatisfiable: two branches each MUST emit 'exactly one' terminal marker on the same carrier, and three others force append-refusal with no marker, with no precedence or already-terminal rule
blockers.subjectQuote: projectPurge: 'MUST append exactly one grant-journal-terminal-marker … and then MUST refuse further appends on that (project, grant generation) carrier.' grantGenerationClosure: 'MUST terminalize the shared journal: emit exactly one grant-journal-terminal-marker and MUST refuse further appends on that carrier.'

measurement.theCarrierIsSharedByBothEvents: lifecycle.carrier defines 'One durable journal per (project, grant generation)'. A given carrier therefore belongs to exactly one project AND one grant generation, so both a project purge and a grant-generation closure can apply to the same carrier at different times. Grant-generation lifecycle is DR-105's and is not tied to project purge, so neither event implies the other.
measurement.theCollision: Whichever fires first emits its mandatory marker and then MUST refuse further appends. When the second fires it MUST emit 'exactly one' marker on a carrier that is already refusing appends — unsatisfiable. If the writer emitted it anyway, the carrier would hold two terminal markers, violating both clauses' 'exactly one'. The block states no precedence, no idempotence, and no 'if already terminal' exemption.
measurement.threeFurtherTerminalStatesHaveNoMarkerAt: lossOrCapacity: 'the writer fail-closes and refuses new appends.' backupRestore: '…that grant generation is permanently revoked: further appends MUST fail-closed.' reversibility: FROZEN-UNDER-OVERTURN bytes take 'no new appends'. Each reaches a permanent append-refusing state WITHOUT a terminal marker. Any subsequent projectPurge or grantGenerationClosure on that carrier still MUST emit one — again unsatisfiable. And because grantGenerationClosure defines terminalization AS marker emission, a generation that is 'permanently revoked' by restore is terminal by one definition and un-terminalized by the other.
measurement.whatCodexAskedFor: SCC-V6-B1's repair text: 'Specify deterministic, separate behavior for operation purge, project purge, and grant-generation closure; IDENTIFY WHICH EVENT, IF ANY, TERMINALIZES the shared journal and make refusal after terminalization mandatory.' The separation and the mandatory refusal are delivered. The singular identification is not: two events terminalize and three more silently produce terminal states.
measurement.operationPurgeIsNotTheProblem: operationPurge is correctly excluded — 'MUST NOT terminalize … MAY append an operation-scoped closure record … Further appends for other operations on the same generation remain lawful.' That clause is coherent and I am not attacking it.

blockers.whyBlocker: The lifecycle is labelled 'DESIGN-ANSWERED for the carrier and the named branches below', and the DR-124 row's acceptance cell requires custody, backup/purge/migration rules. A harness author implementing these branches literally reaches a state where a MUST cannot be discharged, and the artifact gives no rule for choosing. This is not a disclosure gap that a reader can route around: it is an internal contradiction among mandatory clauses added this generation, in the exact area the OBJECT was raised about. It also matters beyond drafting, because 'exactly one terminal marker' is what makes a closed carrier distinguishable from a truncated one — the anti-tail-loss property backupRestore depends on. If a carrier can end up with zero markers (loss, restore-revocation, overturn) or be required to hold two, that distinguishing property is not established.
blockers.whatIsNotWrong: The direction is right and each clause is individually sensible. Making terminalization mandatory was my v6 S-2 repair and it landed; separating the three purge scopes was Codex's and it landed; fail-closed at loss and revocation-on-possible-tail-loss are the correct conservative answers. Nothing here asks for a weaker rule — only for the branches to be made mutually consistent.
blockers.minimumRepair: State a single terminalization rule for the carrier and make every other branch defer to it. Concretely: define terminal as a property of the carrier, not of an event; say that the FIRST of {project purge, grant-generation closure} to occur MUST emit the one marker and that any later such event on an already-terminal carrier is a no-op rather than a second MUST; and state whether the marker-less terminal states (lossOrCapacity, restore-revocation, FROZEN-UNDER-OVERTURN) are terminal without a marker or must be marked when the writer next becomes able. Then reconcile grantGenerationClosure's definition of terminalization with backupRestore's 'permanently revoked'.

shouldFix.title: Sequence numbers are defined per-carrier and restart at origin, yet two clauses forbid 'reusing' a closed generation's sequence numbers — the no-reuse rule is either vacuous or violated at the first record
shouldFix.subjectQuote: grantGenerationClosure: 'A new grant generation, if any, is a new carrier with sequence restarting at its own origin and MUST NOT reuse the closed generation's sequence numbers.' backupRestore: 'Continuation is only a new grant generation without sequence reuse.'
shouldFix.measurement: lifecycle.carrier states 'The next sequence number is derived solely from the durable journal tail of that carrier', which makes sequence strictly per-carrier — consistent with permission-truth-tables.v6, whose linearization gives 'ONE durable, append-only grant journal per (project, grant generation)' with 'a strictly increasing unsigned integer sequence number assigned by the single writer'. A new carrier has an empty tail, so its first record takes the origin value, which the closed carrier also used. Under that reading the new generation reuses the closed generation's sequence VALUES at its first record, contradicting 'MUST NOT reuse'; under the alternative reading — that identity is the (generation, sequence) pair — the no-reuse clause is trivially satisfied and states nothing. The artifact does not say which it means, while invoking 'sequence reuse' twice as a hazard to be prevented.
shouldFix.whatIsNotWrong: The intent is clear and correct: a continued generation must not be confusable with the closed one, which is the right anti-replay posture and the reason backupRestore refuses to continue in place. The carrier rule itself is accurate against permission-truth-tables.v6.
shouldFix.whyItStillMatters: The no-reuse clause is doing real work in backupRestore — it is the guarantee that a revoked generation cannot be silently continued after possible tail loss. If it is vacuous, that guarantee rests on the generation identifier alone and should say so; if it is not vacuous, then 'restarting at its own origin' is wrong and the origin must be derived from the closed generation's high-water mark, which the artifact expressly declines to mint a witness for. A reader cannot tell which property is being promised.
shouldFix.minimumRepair: State the scope of sequence identity once: either that sequence numbers are carrier-scoped and uniqueness is carried by the (project, grant generation, sequence) triple — in which case say 'MUST NOT continue the closed generation's carrier' rather than 'MUST NOT reuse its sequence numbers' — or that numbers must not repeat across generations, in which case name what supplies the new origin given that no high-water witness is minted.

coordinatorNote: The architecture has been settled since v4; what this round changed is the depth of the grant-journal lifecycle, and that depth is where the blocker now lives. I want the coordinator to read B-1 as a consequence of good work rather than a regression: v6 had a lifecycle that was too thin to contradict itself, and v7's is detailed enough that its branches can be checked against each other — and three of them cannot all hold. The fix is small and local. Define terminal as a property of the carrier rather than of an event, make the second terminalizing event a no-op on an already-terminal carrier, and say whether the marker-less terminal states must later be marked. Nothing about the supersession, the owner set, the D-096 (A) gate, or the placement needs to move. S-1 is the third appearance of one recurring habit and the repair I would suggest is structural rather than another re-point: make the live-pointer fields name 'the reMeasurementAt* object whose standing is LIVE' so they cannot go stale when v8 adds another. S-2 is a one-sentence clarification of what 'sequence reuse' means. I did not read the other current v7 reviewer, did not edit the subject, file 08, or COORDINATOR-DECISIONS.md, did not apply SUP-124-GRANT-JOURNAL, did not mint a D-096 (A) grant, did not treat SC-OPS as a grant journal outside the subject's named supersession, and did not commit.
